passage: Sunday. Been thinking about what happens to the evening reading circle if I take the Pune job next year, or just get swamped at work. Right now it's me: I hold the key, the booklist and the phone numbers. That isn't a project, it's a habit of mine. So this month I asked Minakshi, who lives two lanes from the hall and comes every day, to start opening up and leading the story hour. Showed how the register works, where the books go, who to call about the hall. Also asked five parents for a small monthly amount, enough for the hall's electricity bill. Four said yes. On Thursday Minakshi read to the kids alone while I stood outside. It wobbled, and it worked. — Manoj

qa.q: How many parents said yes to giving a small monthly amount?

qa.a: Manoj is worried that the reading circle depends on Manoj alone, so it is a personal habit and not yet a lasting project.

qa.q: What other step could help the circle carry on without Manoj?
qa.a: Manoj could write a one-page handover with the steps for opening up, the register and the hall contacts, so any volunteer could follow it.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt reading to the children alone while Manoj stood outside?
qa.a: Minakshi was probably nervous but trusted, since it wobbled and then worked.

grounding: Shows a person asking who will run the reading circle when they are busy or away, training a local volunteer and arranging small monthly funding.

passage:
Anand: Uma, got the Pune offer. Joining in six weeks 😅
Uma: Congrats!! And the Sunday reading corner?
Anand: That's what kept me up. Right now it runs only because I unlock the room and carry the books.
Anand: If I get sick for one month, it just stops. That isn't a library, that's me.
Uma: So what are you thinking?
Anand: You already know every kid's name. Could you run it with me for the next five Sundays? You do everything, I only watch.
Uma: Okay, but the chai, chart paper, new books?
Anand: Ten parents said they'd give a small amount each month. I'll open a shared record so anyone can see it, not only me.
Uma: And the key?
Anand: Second key goes to you and one to the society office 🙏
Uma: Fine. Sunday I'm in charge 🙂

qa.q: How many Sundays does Anand ask Uma to run the corner alongside?
qa.a: Anand asks Uma to run it together for the next five Sundays, with Anand only watching.

qa.q: What was Anand worried about on getting the Pune offer?
qa.a: Anand was anxious that the reading corner would stop, since it runs only because Anand unlocks the room and carries the books.

qa.q: What else could Anand add to the handover plan, and why?
qa.a: Anand could write a one-page guide on how a Sunday runs, so Uma or any new helper is not relying on memory after the move.

qa.q: How might Uma see the plan to hand the corner over?
qa.a: Uma may feel trusted but a little pressured, and the five practice Sundays, the second key and the shared money record make it feel possible rather than dumped on Uma.

grounding: It shows a young organiser about to move away asking who will keep the project going, training a local helper and arranging small monthly contributions so it does not rest on one person.

passage:
The seed library in Kharkhoda's panchayat hall was only a steel cupboard and a register, but forty families now swapped seeds there each sowing season. Simran had built it over two years. Now the nursing post in the district hospital was hers, and she would be there six days a week.
Sitting on the hall steps, she counted on her fingers. Who opens the cupboard in June when I'm on a night shift? Who writes in the register? Who buys the paper packets when they run out?
Arnab, the dairy man's son, had helped her sort millet seeds every Saturday. That week she stood beside him while he filled the register himself. Then she went to the milk cooperative meeting and asked if a small share of each month's fund could buy packets and ink. The members agreed.
"Now it belongs to the village," Arnab said.

qa.q: Where was the seed library kept?
qa.a: It was a steel cupboard and a register in Kharkhoda's panchayat hall.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling as she counted on her fingers on the hall steps?
qa.a: She was worried that the library would fall apart once she was on night shifts, and she was checking each job that only she did.

qa.q: Which other step could make the library even safer if Arnab also becomes busy?
qa.a: Training a second helper alongside Arnab would help, so the cupboard and register never depend on one person again.

qa.q: How might the milk cooperative members see Simran's request?
qa.a: They may feel the library is now partly theirs, because a small share of their monthly fund keeps it stocked, which gives them a reason to protect it.

grounding: It shows a woman leaving for a job who asks who will run her seed library, trains a local helper and arranges small monthly funding from the cooperative.
